newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra ends infrastructure bonds scheme.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra ends infrastructure bonds scheme.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said on Friday the government would introduce legislation into parliament to prevent any more investors gaining access to the infrastructure bonds tax break.

The responsible bureau, the Development Allowance Authority, had examined the system, which was intended to promote private infrastructure investment, and found that it was being exploited for tax minimisation, Costello said in a statement.

"This examination has revealed that schemes being proposed are exploiting the concession for tax-minimisation schemes and these additional taxation benefits are principally being accessed by financial by packagers and high marginal tax rate investors," he said.
Applications pending would mean A$4 billion in lost tax to the government over three years if approved, he said.
The legislation would end the scheme from Friday and most of the pending applications would not be granted, he said. Developments already approved would be unaffected.
The former Labor government announced infrastructure bonds as part of its 1992 strategy to pump-prime the then ailing economy.
If the authority approves a particular project, the developer can issue bonds whose interest attracts no tax.
Lenders therefore offer a lower interest rate and although the developer cannot claim the interest expense against income the bottom line is a tax-break for the approved project.
The policy change would have not affect on the forward estimates of the government's finances, he said.
Rather, the continuing issue of infrastructure bonds would have cost more than allowed for in the forward estimates.
Costello said some new scheme would be introduced but gave no details.
"In the (May) budget context, the government will consider a number of alternative arrangements for continuing our support for genuine infrastructure investment whilst eliminating abuse."
Costello effectively suspended the scheme in September, telling the authority to accept no more applications.
The new legislation would also prevent changes to the financing for approved developments to increase tax benefits, he said.
The authority had already approved projects with borrowings totalling A$4.0 billion.
The government does not quite control the upper house of parliament, the Senate, but Costello told reporters he thought that one of the minor parties, the Democrats, would support the policy change.
